topic.name: Double Integrals Over Type I Regions

question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_{1/2}^{1} \int_{1/x}^{4x} y \,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx &= \int_{1/2}^{1} \left[\int_{1/x}^{4x} y \,\mathrm dy \right]\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{1/2}^{1}\left(\bigg[ \dfrac{y^2}{2} \bigg]_{1/x}^{4x} \right)\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{1/2}^{1}\left( 8x^2 - \dfrac{1}{2x^2} \right)\,\mathrm dx \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{1/2}^{1}\left( 8x^2 - \dfrac{1}{2x^2} \right)\,\mathrm dx &=\left[\dfrac{8}{3}x^3 + \dfrac{1}{2x} \right]_{1/2}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac{8}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} \right) - \left( \dfrac{1}{3} + 1 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{11}{6} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $y=3-x,$ $y=0,$ and $x=0,$ as shown above, then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} ye^{x} \, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region.

  • To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 3-x &= 0 \\[3pt] x &= 3 \end{align*} So, $x$-limits are $ 0 \le x \le 3. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 3-x \big\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D ye^{x} \,\mathrm{d}A &=\int_0^3 \int_{0}^{3-x} ye^{x} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

example.title: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A,$ where $D$ is the finite region below the line $y=2$ enclosed by the lines $y=x$ and $x=0.$
question.explanation:
Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

  • We already know the intersection of the line $y=x$ with the line $y=2.$ So, the $x$-limits are $ 0 \le x \le 2. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region:

\[ D = \Big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \quad x \leq y \leq 2 \Big\} \]

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

\[ \iint \limits_{D} y^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{0}^2 \int_x^{2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \]

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^2 \int_x^{2} y^2\,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_{0}^2 \left[ \int_x^{2} y^2 \, \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^2 \left[ \dfrac{y^3}{3} \right]_x^{2} \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^2 \left( \dfrac{8}{3}- \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right) \,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^2 \left( \dfrac{8}{3}- \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right) \,\mathrm{d}x &= \left[ \dfrac{8x}{3} - \dfrac{x^4}{12} \right]_{0}^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3} - 0 \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the line $y=4$ and the curve $y=x^2,$ as shown above, then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{x+y} \, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region.

  • To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 4 &= x^2 \\[5pt] x^2-4 &= 0 \\[5pt] (x-2)(x+2)&=0 \end{align*} So, $x$-limits are $ -2 \le x \le 2. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 2, \quad x^2 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D e^{x+y} \,\mathrm{d}A &=\int_{-2}^2 \int_{x^2}^{4} e^{x+y} \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

example.title: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given

question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_0^{2}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} y \,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{2} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}}y \,\mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2} \left[ \dfrac{y^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} \, \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2} \left(\dfrac{4-x^2}{2} - 0 \right) \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{2} \left(2 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_0^{2} \left(2 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) \mathrm{d}x &= \left[2x - \dfrac{x^3}{6}\right]_0^{2} \\[5pt] &= 2(2) - \dfrac{2^3}{6} - 0 \\[5pt] &= 4 - \dfrac{4}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{3} \end{align*}
